E1226.summary: The single subject from which, after the Smaragdine (Emerald) Table, all things proceed by adaptation; Atwood identifies it with the Identity made in regeneration and, later, with our psychical essence.
E1226.body:
The term comes from the Hermetic Table, cited as the Smaragdine, Emerald or Smagardine Table (also as the Smaragdine Tablet of Thrice Great Hermes): it speaks of “for performing the miracles of the One Thing whence all the rest proceed by adaptation” [III.1 ¶41; cf. I.1 ¶9, I.2 ¶48]. The Table as quoted makes the Sun its father, the Moon its mother, the Wind its carrier and the Earth its nurse, and says “This is the father of all perfection and consummation of the whole world.” [IV.2 ¶44]. A quoted master, whom Atwood follows, says “the whole matter I know to be One only Thing” [III.1 ¶21]; in that passage folly, phantasy, passion and Reason are its modes of being.

Boehme, as quoted, says the first something was “a certain cloud or darkness, which was condensed into water”, and that “this water is that One Thing in which all things are contained” [III.2 ¶15]. Atwood takes this up herself: “God of nothing created something which was made that one thing in which are all”, and she adds that “this One Thing appears to be nothing less or more than that Identity which is made in the regeneration” [III.2 ¶16]. For the creature it is the first divine manifestation out of the abyss.

Atwood says that “The same tradition of the manifold powers and preservation of the One Thing runs in symbol” through the Gentile Mythology [III.3 ¶69]. The verses she quotes make it the only key to the sealed Art (“Which one thing only can unlocke; This one things learn to know,” [III.3 ¶68]) and “A mass confused and darkly clad, That in itself, all Nature had”, called “The first Material Mother of all.” [III.3 ¶76]. The verses call it indestructible, easy to find and hard to get.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says plainly: “The One Thing; it is our psychical essence; our nervous system.” [APP ¶176].

E1227.summary: An unnamed authority (“says one”) whom Atwood cites in the Table Talk to support her claim that everything depends on the will and the intention.
E1227.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), an unnamed authority is quoted in support of the point that all depends on the willing and the intention: “That which in the hands of fools is nothing in that of a philosopher becomes to be all in all” [APP ¶35].

E1228.summary: Atwood's name for philosophy in the true sense: the knowledge of true Being that was the object of initiation.
E1228.body: Atwood equates the two terms directly: “philosophy, that is to say, Ontological Wisdom” [II.2 ¶4]. She calls it “the Wisdom of true Being” [II.2 ¶5]. In that passage it is the knowledge that initiation aimed at.

E1229.summary: In Agrippa's phrase, the worker of all wonderful effects, which is located within us.
E1229.body: Atwood quotes Agrippa: “in us is the Operator of all wonderful effects” [II.1 ¶26]. The Operator is inward, not an outside agent.

E1230.summary: A principle that, once freed, draws the mind's other faculties into its vortex, revels with them until satiated, and is then more easily ensnared.
E1230.body: Atwood says the faculties are “drawn away afterwards into the vortex of the Opposive Principle, rapidly attracting them when it is freed” [III.1 ¶66]. It revels with them, becomes satiated and is then more easily ensnared. She illustrates this with Orpheus's tale of Saturn bound in fetters while drunk [III.1 ¶66]. The text does not say outright that this is the same as the ‘rebellious Principle’ of III.1 ¶64.

E1231.summary: An oracle of Apollo, taken from Eusebius, used as the epigraph of II.2: the path to Deity is hard, and the Egyptians and other ancient peoples disclosed it.
E1231.body: Atwood uses it as an epigraph: “The Path by which to Deity we climb Is arduous, rough, ineffable, sublime;” [II.2 ¶1]. The verses go on to say the path was disclosed by the Egyptians and other ancient peoples.

E1232.summary: The oracle given to Amelius, which Atwood quotes to show the place where the soul of Plotinus dwells.
E1232.body: Atwood quotes the oracle given to Amelius about where the soul of Great Plotinus is. It describes the place in Latin: “Ubi Amicitia est, ubi cupido visu mollis” [II.4 ¶11, II.4 ¶12] (ours: where Friendship is, where desire is gentle to behold).

E1233.summary: Oracular sayings that Atwood cites often, including the Oracula Chaldaica and Zoroastri Oracula, to support her teaching on the soul's ascent, the formless Fire, purification and piety.
E1233.body:
Atwood treats the oracles as supporting authorities. One urges the soul to turn upward, away from the image-loving Hades: “Let the immortal depth of thy soul be predominant, and all thy eyes extend upwards” [II.3 ¶26, II.3 n27; footnote cites Zoroastri Oracula, Anima, Corpus, Homo]. Another, from the Oracula Chaldaica, names the true vision as the formless Fire: “When thou seest a Fire without Form, Shining flashingly through the depths of the World, Hear the voice of Fire” [II.3 ¶46–47, II.3 n50]. It is cited again for the Fire as the derivation and dispenser of Fire [II.3 ¶52–53].

The Oracle also gives the name ‘Pratum’ (meadow) to the meadow of Divine Ideas [II.4 ¶9]. It warns about the infinite End of the principle: “Stoop not down, for a precipice lies below in the earth” [III.2 ¶15]. The oracles are said to teach that the impure perceptive medium needs ‘alternation and solution’ before it can tell good from evil [II.2 ¶15]. On piety, Atwood writes: “Thus piety is available for all things, as the oracles declare” [III.4 ¶22]. In that passage prayer is piety's chief exercise and is profitable for great undertakings. With Julian, the oracles support the claim that “through purifying ceremonies bodies become worthy of receiving divine assistance and health” [IV.3 ¶30–31, IV.3 n10]. An oracle is also reported to have called Socrates the wisest of mankind because of that Nothing [IV.4 ¶27].

E1234.summary: In Clemens Alexandrinus's words as Atwood quotes them, the rites or celebrations of the Mysteries.
E1234.body: Atwood quotes Clemens Alexandrinus: “These are the orgies of the Mysteries” [II.2 ¶5]. The word means the Mysteries' rites.

E1235.summary: The adepts' figure of an animal that must be skinned by the Hand; in the Table Talk, Atwood explains it as the opposite will clothed in Light.
E1235.body:
In III.1, Atwood reports the adepts' saying: “For the Orient Animal must be stripped of his skin, not with arrows or clubs, but with the Hand, as Adepts say” [III.1 ¶64]. The skin is a lion's skin. The Latin in that passage adds that the animal then enters the great salt sea and comes out again with beauty. The figure is not explained there.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood herself gives the meaning: “The ‘orient animal’ means the animal (that is, the opposite) will which is clothed in Light”. She also calls it “the third which rises in opposition to the first” [APP ¶21].

E1236.summary: A Hermetic expression quoted from Hermes: two oriental quicksilvers that hunt the sulphurs and contain the bodies.
E1236.body: Hermes, as quoted, speaks of “the fat of the two oriental quicksilvers, which hunt the sulphurs and contain the bodies” [I.3 ¶20]. The text does not explain the expression further.

E1237.summary: Named in the story about Ammonius.
E1237.body: Origen is named only in the story of Ammonius [III.2 ¶64].

E1238.summary: Nature's Original Light: the infallible touchstone by which the capable can tell what is rationally possible.
E1238.body: Atwood speaks of Nature's “infallible touchstone of her Original Light” [IV.3 ¶54]. The able use it to discern what is rationally possible.

E1239.summary: The state to which bodies must be reduced, by introversion of the generated life, before they can be truly manifested and made permanent.
E1239.body: Atwood names as a condition of true manifestation and permanence “the reduction of bodies to their original matter, by introversion of the generated life” [I.2 ¶49].

E1240.summary: An evil that is overcome by subtle stratagems, after which the New Life arises.
E1240.body: Atwood writes: “The evil of the Original Sin being overcome by so many subtle stratagems” [III.1 ¶66], after which the New Life arises. The context suggests that the stratagems are those just described for ensnaring the Opposive Principle.

E1241.summary: The real power that the types signify; without understanding it and cooperating with it, the types only mimic efficacy.
E1241.body: Atwood says the types need “a true understanding and cooperation of that original virtue, apart from which they do but mimic an efficacy” [I.1 ¶26].

E1242.summary: An authority whom Atwood cites often for mythic illustrations that she reads hermetically: Pan, the Cave of Mercury, Saturn's fettering, and the Day that follows the Night.
E1242.body:
Atwood quotes Orpheus to illustrate Pan as the whole of nature: “Fortis subtilis Pan, integer et generalis” [I.2 ¶28, I.2 n26, Orpheus Hymni] (ours: strong, subtle Pan, whole and universal). From the Argonautics she cites prudent entry into the Cave of Mercury (“Mercurii ingedier spuluncam” [III.1 ¶17–18]), which she interprets hermetically. In the same vein, Orpheus is said to have recommended taking the Hermetic material in the cave of Mercury [III.2 ¶7].

She draws on Orpheus for the tale of Saturn, bound in fetters while drunk by his son through a stratagem: “and by the advice of the goddess, too, according to Orpheus, the subtle stratagem was contrived” [III.1 ¶66]. It illustrates how the satiated Opposive Principle is ensnared. She also cites ‘the Day of Orpheus’, which follows the Night [III.2 ¶28].

E1243.summary: An emblem work (Emblema LVI) that Atwood cites to support the point that the corrupt mind cannot draw the healthful waters.
E1243.body: Atwood cites the Apodosis of Emblema LVI: “Cui scelerum viru mens moribunda tumet” [III.3 ¶11–12, III.3 n5] (ours: whose dying mind swells with the poison of crimes). It supports her point that a corrupt mind cannot draw the healthful waters.

E1244.summary: An Orphic fragment that Atwood cites on purity and contemplation of the One, while qualifying its claim that He is never seen by mortal eyes.
E1244.body: The fragment opens: “I open a secret to the Initiated, but let the doors be shut.” [II.4 ¶40, II.4 n28]. Atwood uses it in support of purity and contemplation of the One. She qualifies its statement that He is ‘never seen by mortal eyes’: the Initiated, she says, did behold Him.

E1245.summary: Cited for the teaching that Pan, of necessity, evolves every property and form out of his central will.
E1245.body: Atwood cites the Orphic oracles in support of the teaching that Pan evolves every property and form out of his central will, of necessity [I.2 ¶36].

E1246.summary: An unnamed Orphic poet, quoted in Latin, on what blessed Eurotas heard while Phoebus (Apollo) meditated.
E1246.body: Atwood quotes the Orphic poet's verse on Apollo contemplating such rivers: “Omnia quae Phoebo quondam meditante beatus Audiit Eurotas” [II.4 ¶13–14] (ours: all that blessed Eurotas once heard while Phoebus meditated).

E1247.summary: An Orphic verse cited for the radiant return of Bacchus.
E1247.body: The verse shows Bacchus returning “triumphant, and appearing in splendour to mortals” [II.4 ¶54].

E1248.summary: The offspring that the Matter brings forth by the Fire of nature, lawfully conceived; Atwood calls it the Philosophic Sun.
E1248.body: Atwood says what the Matter brings forth by the lawfully conceived Fire of nature “is Orus, the Philosophic Sun” [III.3 ¶62].

E1249.summary: In the fable, the brother whom Typhon kills and scatters; applied to the work, Atwood identifies him with the Divine Light, the foreign body of Light.
E1249.body: In the fable, Typhon kills Osiris and scatters his body. Applying it to the work, Atwood identifies Osiris with “the foreign body of Light, which is Osiris” [III.1 ¶56] and “Osiris, i.e., the Divine Light” [III.1 ¶63]. The Efficient reduces this Light to vapor, and it suffers restraint as it passes through the voluntary axle [III.1 ¶56–63].

E1250.summary: A Persian sage who, as Atwood reports from Pliny, first brought the Persian spirit into Greece.
E1250.body: Citing Pliny, Atwood names Ostanes as the Persian sage who first brought the Persian spirit into Greece [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n13].

E1251.summary: Unnamed philosophers reported as teaching that the White Mercury is the bath of the Moon and the Red Mercury the bath of the Sun.
E1251.body: The speaker reports others as saying “the White Mercury is the bath of the Moon, and that the Red Mercury is the bath of the Sun” [IV.3 ¶10]. The speaker does not dispute this but adds to it.

E1252.summary: Earlier masters who, Hermes says, veiled the secret in figures, which he claims he will now open.
E1252.body: Hermes, as quoted, says the secrets “are given by our ancestors in figures and types” [I.3 ¶50]. He claims to open them.

E1253.summary: The author of The Triumph, cited for listing the fixed principles: the Elements, the Three Principles, white and citrine Mercury, and fixed Sulphur as the Stone.
E1253.body: This author is cited for a list of the fixed principles: the Elements, the Three Principles, white and citrine Mercury, and fixed Sulphur as the Stone. The list begins: “you must make the conversion of the Elements” [IV.2 ¶6].

E1254.summary: Cited for the view that the Art is perfected by multiplying the Prester and placing him in the supreme Ether.
E1254.body: ‘Our doctors’ are cited in support of the view that the Art's perfection lies in multiplying the Prester and placing him in the supreme Ether [II.3 ¶56].

E1255.summary: In Sendivogius's words, the source of the water and the salt-nitre, holding a river of living water.
E1255.body: Sendivogius, as quoted, speaks of “Our Earth in which there is a river of living water” [IV.3 ¶21]. It is the source of the water and the salt-nitre. The text does not define it further.
